claims.text: Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C for full densification.
Conventional single-phase ZrB2 lacks inherent oxidation protection.
Conventional single-phase ZrB2 lacks inherent protection against liquid plating-metal corrosion.
A controlled CVD or solution-based process can reproducibly create thin, uniform Si-rich shells on ZrB2 powders.
Si-containing additives can facilitate consolidation of difficult-to-sinter ultra-high-temperature boride and carbide powders.
Si-containing additives can improve the oxidation resistance and mechanical properties of ultra-high-temperature boride and carbide systems.
Spark plasma sintering of Si-rich core-shell ZrB2 powders under inert atmosphere can achieve consolidation below 1700 °C.
The Si-rich shell forms a transient liquid phase during consolidation.
The transient liquid phase promotes early neck formation and bonding between ZrB2 cores.
The Si-rich shell promotes full densification of ZrB2 cores at temperatures below 1700 °C.
Residual Si or Si-containing reaction products oxidize in service to form a continuous borosilicate scale.
The borosilicate scale passivates ZrB2 against further high-temperature oxidation.
The borosilicate scale impedes corrosion by liquid plating metals.
The engineered powders will achieve near-full density below 1700 °C.
The low-temperature core-shell material will have mechanical properties comparable to or better than ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C.
The core-shell material will exhibit significantly better oxidation durability than conventional single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
The core-shell material will exhibit significantly better resistance to liquid plating-metal corrosion than both comparison materials.
Parallel synthesis of boride and SiC composite constituents can produce strong interfaces.
